questions.question: Which pancreatic cell type primarily produces insulin?
questions.explanation: Pancreatic beta cells release insulin in response to rising blood glucose. Alpha cells primarily produce glucagon.

questions.question: Which mechanism best explains typical type 1 diabetes?
choices: Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells
questions.explanation: Type 1 diabetes is driven by autoimmune beta-cell destruction, causing severe insulin deficiency and risk for ketosis and DKA.

questions.question: Which statement best describes early typical type 2 diabetes?
choices: Complete absence of insulin from onset
Insulin resistance with compensatory insulin production
questions.explanation: Type 2 diabetes usually begins with insulin resistance. The pancreas may initially compensate with more insulin, followed by progressive beta-cell dysfunction.

questions.question: Why can severe hyperglycemia cause polyuria and polydipsia?
choices: Glucose in urine causes osmotic diuresis and water loss
questions.explanation: When renal glucose reabsorption is exceeded, glucose remains in urine and retains water in the tubules: glucosuria causes osmotic diuresis, polyuria, and thirst.

questions.question: A patient with DKA has an initially elevated serum potassium. Which interpretation is most accurate?
choices: Total-body potassium must also be high
The patient may have marked total-body potassium depletion despite a high serum value
Insulin will move potassium out of cells
questions.explanation: Insulin deficiency and acidosis can shift potassium out of cells, while osmotic diuresis and vomiting cause potassium loss. Potassium can fall rapidly during treatment.

questions.question: A patient with diabetes has vomiting, abdominal pain, dehydration, tachypnea, and positive ketones. What is the most appropriate general disposition?
choices: Treat only the glucose value in clinic
Emergency evaluation for a hyperglycemic crisis
questions.explanation: This presentation is concerning for DKA or another hyperglycemic emergency. It requires urgent evaluation with monitored fluids, electrolytes, ketones, and acid-base status.

questions.question: TSH is 12 mIU/L and free T4 is low in a patient with fatigue, cold intolerance, and constipation. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.explanation: In primary hypothyroidism, the failing thyroid produces too little hormone, so free T4 is low and pituitary TSH rises through loss of negative feedback.

questions.question: A patient has weight loss, tremor, palpitations, suppressed TSH, and elevated free T4. Which pattern is most consistent?
questions.explanation: Primary hyperthyroidism produces excess thyroid hormone, which suppresses TSH by negative feedback and increases metabolic and adrenergic symptoms.

questions.question: Which laboratory pattern best fits primary adrenal insufficiency?
choices: High aldosterone with hypokalemia in every case
questions.explanation: When the adrenal cortex fails, cortisol falls and pituitary ACTH rises. Aldosterone may also be deficient, contributing to volume depletion and hyperkalemia.

questions.question: A patient with known adrenal insufficiency develops vomiting, profound weakness, confusion, and hypotension during an infection. What is the priority FNP decision?
choices: Wait for outpatient cortisol testing before acting
Recognize possible adrenal crisis and arrange emergency evaluation
questions.explanation: Hypotension, gastrointestinal symptoms, weakness, and altered mental status during physiologic stress may signal adrenal crisis. Emergency treatment is required; it is not safe to manage as a routine outpatient issue.
